And where something does appear to help you, the nurturing belongs in reality to the one being on whom both of you depend in order to exist at all.

**The fact you cannot dispute.**

What follows the command is evidence, and the sources keep pointing at how ordinary it is. Al-Jalālayn glosses *Who created you* as: made you when you were nothing. Tanwīr al-Miqbās supplies the lineage — created you as different lineages beginning from a drop of sperm, and those before you just as He created those who came before you. Maʿārif puts the weight on what the verb cannot mean here: giving existence to what did not exist before, and producing, out of the darkness and filth of a mother's womb, a creature as lovely and noble as a human being. That is a quality nobody can even imagine belonging to anything created. Tazkīr al-Qurʾān explains why people nevertheless do exactly that. Because God is invisible, a man gives importance to some visible object and worships that instead of God. He equates the created with the Creator — sometimes a part of creation, sometimes its entirety — at times calling it by the name of God, and at times doing so without taking God's name at all. Therein, in that source's phrase, lies man's basic error: he has become so attached to what he has elevated that he cannot believe it is unreal, and cannot believe that the truth is being pronounced by a mortal like himself. Ibn Kathīr records that several scholars of tafsīr, ar-Rāzī among them, used these verses as the proof for the existence of the Creator, and he brings the reply of a bedouin asked for his evidence: the camel's dung testifies to the camel and a track testifies that someone has walked — a sky holding the giant stars, a land with its fairways, a sea with its waves, do these not testify that the Most Kind, the All-Knowing, exists?

**Only "those before you".**

The verse says *and those before you* and stops. It does not say and those who come after you, and Maʿārif draws a consequence from the silence that most readers pass over: by mentioning only what came before, the verse signals that there will be no community to succeed the community of the Prophet ﷺ, since no prophet will be sent down after the last one, and therefore no new *ummah* will arise. The address to humanity is then not the first in a series but the last — which is one reason the verses that follow will not soften the claim.

**What the closing clause is doing.**

*So that you may become mindful* is the part a reader skims, and the sources slow him down. Al-Jalālayn makes the grammatical observation that decides how much weight the clause can carry: *laʿalla*, rendered as "so that", is essentially a word of hoping, an optative — but when it is spoken by God it denotes an affirmative. Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the clause as rescue: so that you may save yourselves from suffering, by following His instructions and keeping away from what He has prohibited. Tanwīr al-Miqbās: so that you may ward off His wrath and torment, and obey Him. Maʿārif records the alternative renderings — so that you may save yourselves from hell, or guard yourselves against evil — and then closes the argument: salvation and paradise are to be hoped for only where Allah is worshipped alone and no one is associated with Him. What the verse ends on is therefore not a reward appended to a demand. It is the claim that this obedience is what makes a person secure. Maʿārif presses further, and it is the last thing it says on the verse: the oneness of God stated here is not a theory but the only effective way of making a human being fully human. The man whose mind and heart hold it, it says, fears nobody and expects nothing from anybody — shower him with gold or put him in irons and he is unmoved, because he knows where both come from.

22.text:
The argument now comes down to the room you are standing in. *Who has made the earth a place of settlement for you and the sky a canopy* — then rain, then fruit, then *a provision for you*. Four things, and not one of them was made by anyone reading the verse. So the verse draws its single prohibition, and it draws it as something the audience has already settled: *do not knowingly set up equals to Allah*. The sting is in that adverb. It is not saying that they have been told the wrong thing, or that they lack the evidence. It is saying they have the evidence, and know they have it.

**The four blessings, and how to read them.**

The first word is worth pausing on. Al-Jalālayn glosses *a place of settlement* as a couch, like a carpet laid out — and then adds the detail that makes it a designed thing rather than a poetical one: neither extremely hard nor extremely soft, so as to make it impossible to stand firm on it. Al-Mukhtaṣar has the same image, the earth like a carpet spread out in front of you, with the sky masterfully constructed over you. Tanwīr al-Miqbās reads *resting-place* as a place for dwelling and sleeping, and the canopy as raised high above. Maʿārif supplies the proportion between them: the earth is neither soft and fluid like water, on which nothing settles, nor hard like stone or steel, which could not be harnessed for human purposes, but has been given a middle state so that daily life is possible in it. The same source settles a question the word *firash*, something spread out, provokes in a modern reader. It does not imply the earth is flat. The great globe appears flat to an onlooker standing on it, and the Qurʾān's usual way is to describe things in the aspect familiar to an average person, literate or illiterate, townsman or rustic. Tazkīr al-Qurʾān draws the general point behind the list: the world is not inert machinery. It has been invested with profound significance, and its needs are constantly looked after.

**Where your effort stops.**

Three of the four blessings are of a kind in which human action does not appear at all. Maʿārif presses this, because it is where the argument is decided: there was no sign of man when the earth and the sky already existed, and when clouds and rain were already performing their functions. For those three, not even an ignorant person could fancy that the work belongs to a man, or to an idol, or to any created thing. The fourth is the dangerous one. Fruit looks like the exception, because you can see somebody digging, sowing and weeding. Maʿārif answers that the human part accomplishes nothing beyond removing the hindrances to a plant's birth and growth, and that even the water feeding it is not the farmer's creation — all he does is get it to the plant at the right time and quantity. The Qurʾān's own version of the question is quoted by him: *Have you considered the soil you till? Is it you that give them growth or We?* (56:63–64), and there is one answer to it. Ibn Kathīr adds the detail that rain comes down through the clouds, when they need it, and that the vegetation and fruits are sustenance for people and for their cattle.

**Why this verse follows the last one.**

The two verses are a pair, and Maʿārif shows the seam. Verse 21 listed blessings bearing on the human self; verse 22 lists blessings bearing on the physical environment. The reason for the division is that a person has two dimensions, an inner one (*anfus*) and an outer one (*āfāq*), so that the two verses together encompass, in summary, every kind of blessing that descends on human beings. That is also why both are joined to one command and one prohibition. These two verses, Maʿārif says, sum up what all the Divine Books and all the prophets were sent for.

**What the prohibition actually forbids.**

It is about speech as much as about ritual. Tanwīr al-Miqbās expands the sentence: do not say that Allah has peers, or different forms, or coequals — and then gives a second reading of *when you know*, namely, when you know from your own scripture that Allah has no son, no coequal and no peer. Al-Jalālayn gives the logic in one line: do not set up compeers to God while you know that He is the Creator that you do not create, and that only the One who creates can be God. Al-Mukhtaṣar's wording is the plainest: do not consider others to be equal to Allah, when you know that He alone is worthy of being worshipped. Ibn Kathīr supplies the technical shape of the claim — that this is *tawḥīd* in divinity, and that the verse establishes Allah as Creator, Sustainer, Owner and Provider of this life and everything in it, so that He alone deserves worship. He points to the verse that restates it, *It is He Who has made for you the earth as a dwelling place and the sky as a canopy…* (40:64).

**The worst deed, in the Prophet's ﷺ own words.**

Ibn Kathīr brings the ḥadīth that the two Ṣaḥīḥ collections record from Ibn Masʿūd: he asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ which evil deed is the worst with Allah, and the answer was, to take an equal with Allah while He alone created you. Notice that the reply is not murder or theft, and notice that it explains itself with the verb of the previous verse — *He created you*. The same source adds the question Muʿādh reports the Prophet ﷺ asking his companion: do you know Allah's right upon His servants? They must worship Him alone and refrain from associating anything with Him. And Imām Aḥmad narrates at length from al-Ḥārith al-Ashʿarī the five commands given to Yaḥyā ibn Zakariyyā, of which the first is to worship Allah and not associate anything with Him — illustrated there by a parable that belongs to this verse exactly. A man buys a servant with his own money, and the servant works but hands his earnings to somebody else. Which of you would like that of his own servant? The point of the parable is that the arrangement is not merely ungrateful but a transfer of what is owed, and the ḥadīth names the reason: Allah created you and sustains you, therefore worship Him and associate nothing with Him. Ibn Kathīr grades it ḥasan, and cites the same wording as support for singling Allah out in worship.

**What knowing costs you.**

The clause *while you know* has a counterpart in Maʿārif's treatment of the hope expressed at the end of the previous verse, and he uses it to close a doctrinal gap. Certainty there is put in the language of expectation, in order to make a person realise that no human action brings salvation as a necessary reward. Salvation is by grace; the ability to do good, and faith itself, are signs of that grace rather than causes of it. Which is why the same source is unsympathetic toward stopping at apparent causes. He remarks that a worshipper of energy, if he understood this doctrine, would see that power resides neither in steam nor in electricity, but in the One who made them; and that the greatest philosopher who fails to see it is no better than the rustic who watched a train start at the wave of a green flag and stop at the wave of a red one, and bowed to the flags. People laugh at him because he does not know that flags are signs and that engines move trains; and the man who believes in one God is said to laugh at the wiser heads, because he looks through the steam, the fire and the water to the will that makes them do their work. The consequence, in Maʿārif's closing sentence, is the reason for the whole passage: humanity was placed at the head of creation so that the universe should serve a person while he devotes himself to worship, but some people, out of indolence and ignorance, forget the one God — and then have to serve a billion. The next verse is where the challenge is issued.

23.text:
The last two verses argued from things nobody can make. This one argues from a text nobody can match, and it issues a challenge in the open: *if you are in doubt about what We have revealed to Our servant, then produce a sūrah like it*. Not the whole Book — one chapter. Nor does it ask them to compete alone: *call your helpers other than Allah*, *if what you say is true*. The scale of the concession is the point. Anybody, anything, as much help as they want, against a man they already accuse of making it up. Nobody took it up, and the verse treats that as evidence.

**The same argument, turned around.**

Maʿārif notices that the structure repeats. Verses 21 and 22 affirmed the oneness of God by pointing at acts which no one except Allah can perform — creating the sky and the earth, sending down water, bringing fruit out of it. Verses 23 and 24 affirm prophethood by the same method, with one thing changed: now the evidence is a kind of speech which cannot possibly come from anyone except Allah. As the helplessness of creation before the sky and the earth demonstrates that these are Allah's acts, so helplessness before a single chapter demonstrates that this is Allah's word. The verse also closes the obvious escape route. The failure of one man or one group does not prove that another group could not manage it, so the challenge names the helpers in advance and allows every helper, present and future — Maʿārif remarks that they were, in effect, offered the facility of holding an international workshop.

**How much doubt this verse is talking about.**

The word for doubt here is the same word the second verse of this chapter denied about the Book, and Maʿārif makes it carry weight. Citing Imām Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī, he explains that *rayb* is a hesitation or suspicion with no basis in fact, the kind that a little reflection removes. That is why the Qurʾān says elsewhere that this sort of doubt does not belong to a person of knowledge at all (74:31). So the verse is not addressing an honest seeker weighing evidence. It is addressing a suspicion that has no ground and could be dispelled by the one test it refuses to take — and the Book has already announced that there is no *rayb* in it (2:2).

**How small the demand is.**

Al-Jalālayn supplies the definition and the terms: bring a sūrah like it, likewise revealed, and *like it* means in its eloquence, its fine arrangement and its gift of knowledge of the unseen; a sūrah is a passage with a beginning and an end, and it can be as little as three verses. Maʿārif adds the grammar of the mercy: the word *sūrah* means a limited or definite piece, set apart from other passages by divine command, and it appears here without the definite article — so the shortest chapters in the Qurʾān are inside the challenge. Tanwīr al-Miqbās records the opposite emphasis, that they were to produce a sūrah like the sūrah of the Cow, and Al-Jalālayn supplies the taunt that makes the contest fair: do this, for you are fluent speakers of Arabic too.

**Whom they may call.**

The Arabic word is *shuhadāʾ*, witnesses, and Maʿārif derives it: the plural of *shāhid*, one who is present — a witness is called that because he has to be present in court. Then he gives the two referents. Either it means people in general, so that they may summon anyone, from anywhere, or it means the idols of the Makkans, who supposed these blocks of stone would appear on the Day of Judgment to testify in their favour. Ibn Kathīr preserves the early readings in the same order: Ibn ʿAbbās took *your witnesses* to mean aids; Mujāhid took it as wise and eloquent men who would provide the testimony they were seeking; and as-Suddī reported from Abū Mālik that it means partners — go and seek the help of your deities to support you.

**Why the challenge still counts.**

Ibn Kathīr sets this verse inside a series, and the series matters, because the challenge was raised, lowered and raised again. At 17:88 mankind and jinn are invited to combine and produce the like of the Qurʾān; at 11:13 the demand is ten fabricated chapters; at 10:38 and at 28:49 it returns; those were revealed at Makkah, and this one at Madīnah. He reports ar-Rāzī preferring the reading of ʿUmar, Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and the majority — like the Qurʾān as a whole — and praising the generosity of it: individuals and groups, literate and illiterate, were all challenged, which is what makes the challenge complete. The answer to it, in his line, is a question: how can the words of a created being ever be like the words of the Creator? Maʿārif gives the historical verdict. The Makkans were ready to lose their lives to extinguish Islam; the verse offered them the easiest possible way to do it, and wounded their tribal pride by predicting they would fail — and not one contender came forward. Since the challenge has never been withdrawn, he says, the miracle is still on trial, and a miracle that survives to the end of time is worth more than one that ends with the prophet who performed it: every other miracle appeared with its prophet and died with him. That is also why a whole library exists to explain a single word of this verse — al-Jāḥiẓ on the arrangement of the Qurʾān in the third century of Islam, then Wāsiṭī and Ibn ʿĪsā Rabbānī; al-Suyūṭī twice, in al-Itqān and in al-Khaṣāʾiṣ al-Kubrā; Imām Rāzī in his great commentary; Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ; and in this century, al-Rāfiʿī, Rashīd Riḍā and Shabbīr Aḥmad ʿUthmānī. The next verse states what happens to a person who has watched all of that and still refuses.

24.text:
The challenge is answered before anybody attempts it. *But if you are unable to do so—and you will never be able to do so—then fear the Fire fuelled with people and stones.* Two things are said in one breath: you have not managed it, and you never will. The second is a prediction about every generation still to come, made in front of people who were rich, eloquent and furious. And the punishment is not invented for the occasion — the Fire is described as already *prepared*, standing ready for its residents before any of them arrive.

**The prediction inside the verse.**

That clause sits inside the verse as an interruption, and the sources read it as the load-bearing part. Al-Jalālayn marks it as a parenthetical statement and glosses it exactly: because you are incapable, and you will not — never will you be able, because of the Qurʾān's inimitability. Tanwīr al-Miqbās puts the same thing as a warning about attempts rather than intentions: this you can never do, and if you try, you will never succeed. Al-Mukhtaṣar compresses it into a statement of fact: if they are unable to do so — and they will never be able to do it. Ibn Kathīr sees what that costs the doubter, and it is the sharpest remark on the verse: this is itself another miracle, because Allah stated without qualification that the Qurʾān will never be opposed by anything like it, for eternity — a statement which has not been changed up to the present and, he says, shall never change. Maʿārif explains why the threat follows so hard on the heels of a literary contest. The inability is the evidence: once a person has acknowledged that nothing equal to this Book can be produced, and still persists, he is only seeking a place in the Fire.

**What the Fire burns with.**

*Fuelled* is a word with a definition attached to it. Ibn Kathīr: fuel is wood or similar substances used to start and feed a fire, and he cites 72:15, *as for those who deviated, they shall be firewood for Hell*. Then the stones, on which the sources split. The reading he prefers is that they are the giant, rotten, black sulphuric stones which become the hottest things when heated. But, he records, it was also reported that the stones are the idols and rivals that were worshipped instead of Allah, and he gives the verse that settles it: *Certainly you and that which you worship besides Allah are fuel for Hell* (21:98) — you, and the very things you made for yourselves. Tanwīr al-Miqbās takes the material sense, stones of sulphur, and Al-Mukhtaṣar takes the moral one: the Fire burns with the people who deserve the torment and with the idols they used to worship instead of Allah, punishing the worshippers and what they worshipped together. Al-Jalālayn draws the physics out, because for him the stones are the point of the image: the heat is extreme, since this fire burns with stone, unlike the fires of this world, which burn with wood.

**A Fire that already exists.**

The last words of the verse carry a claim about when the Fire exists. Al-Jalālayn notes that *prepared for disbelievers* may be read either as a new sentence or as a circumstance attached to what precedes it; Tanwīr al-Miqbās fills in the sense — created, prepared and preordained. Ibn Kathīr then does something unexpected with a single participle: many of the imams of the Sunnah, he says, used this verse as proof that Jahannam exists now, because Allah said *prepared*, meaning kept in readiness. He supports it with the tradition that the Fire asked its Lord's permission, complaining that some of it had consumed other parts, and was granted two breaths — one in winter and one in summer, which is why the seasons are cold and hot. And he brings the report from Ibn Masʿūd in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim: the companions heard something falling, and the Prophet ﷺ told them it was a stone thrown from the rim of Jahannam seventy years ago, which had only now reached the bottom. That the Fire is prepared, however, is not the same as saying it is indiscriminate. Ibn Isḥāq relays, through ʿIkrimah or Saʿīd bin Jubayr, Ibn ʿAbbās explaining the phrase: prepared for those who embrace the disbelief that you have embraced.

**The only attempt on record.**

The verse also fixes the size of the target, and Ibn Kathīr is explicit that no escape remains here: the challenge in this verse and at 10:38 covers the short sūrahs as much as the long ones, and he knows of no disagreement on that point among scholars, early or late. So the chapter closes the door on "we would have, given a longer passage". One famous attempt is preserved anyway. Before he became Muslim, ʿAmr bin al-ʿĀṣ met Musaylimah, the man nicknamed the Liar, who asked what had recently been revealed to his fellow tribesman in Makkah. ʿAmr said: a short, eloquent sūrah — *By time. Truly, man is in loss* (103:1–2). Musaylimah thought for a while and answered that something similar had been revealed to him too: *O Wabr, O Wabr, you are but two ears and a chest, and the rest of you is unworthy and thin*. ʿAmr's reply is the verdict this verse predicts: by Allah, you know that I know that you are lying. Maʿārif draws the summary: the Makkans were prepared to die to destroy this religion, and the verse offered them the cheapest way to do it and insulted their pride by predicting failure — and history supplies no contender. The next verse turns from the Fire to what the believers are given instead.

25.text:
The chapter turns in a single verse from a fire to a garden. *Give good news ˹O Prophet˺ to those who believe and do good that they will have Gardens under which rivers flow.* Then comes a small scene inside the reward: the residents are handed fruit and say, *this is what we were given before* — and the verse explains that they are being served fruit that looks familiar and tastes different. The last thing it mentions is not scenery but a condition: *they will be there forever*. What the previous verse said of the Fire, that it is prepared, is now said of the Gardens.

**Why these two verses stand together.**

The order is the point, and Ibn Kathīr gives it a name. Having described the torment prepared for those who disbelieve in Him and in His Messengers, Allah now mentions the state of His happy, loyal friends who believe, adhere to the faith and do good deeds — and this alternation, he says, is why the Qurʾān came to be called *mathānī*, the Book that keeps turning: faith mentioned and then disbelief, or the miserable and then the happy, and the other way round, with *tashābah*, likeness, reserved for its recurring themes. Maʿārif puts the hinge plainly: verse 24 spoke of the fire prepared to punish those who do not believe in the Qurʾān, and this verse announces the reward of those who do. Al-Mukhtaṣar notes the change of addressee in the first word — the warnings belonged to the disbelievers, so now the Messenger is told to speak to the believers.

**Rivers, and where they come from.**

*Under which rivers flow* is a phrase the sources take literally and then complicate. Al-Jalālayn parses the image: gardens of trees and habitations, and beneath those trees and palaces the rivers run — and he pauses over the word for river, *nahr*, which is the place through which water flows, so called because the water cuts its channel; the "running" attributed to it is figurative, since the bed runs and the water stands in it. Ibn Kathīr adds what the reports supply: Paradise has rivers running beneath its trees and its rooms, and from the ḥadīth it is learned that they do not run in valleys, as rivers do here. He cites the line Ibn Abī Ḥātim relays from Abū Hurayrah, that the rivers of Paradise spring from beneath hills — or mountains — of musk, and the same saying transmitted from ʿAbdullāh through Masrūq; the sand of Paradise is musk, its stones pearls and jewels, and the banks of al-Kawthar are domes of hollow pearls. Tanwīr al-Miqbās counts the streams: rivers of wine, of milk, of honey and of water.

**The fruit that is not the fruit.**

The strangest moment in the verse is the exclamation. Al-Jalālayn reads *this is what we were given before* as what they were given immediately before this, in Paradise itself, since its fruits resemble one another — and the clause that follows, *they will be served fruit that looks similar*, explains the resemblance as sameness of colour with difference of taste. Ibn Kathīr preserves the version that gives the scene dialogue: Yahyā describes the grass of Paradise as saffron and its hills as musk, and the boys of everlasting youth bringing fruit to the believers; when they are brought something that looks the same, they say this is the same as what you have just brought us, and the answer comes — eat, for the colour is the same but the taste is different. Abū al-ʿĀliyah, relayed by Ar-Rabīʿ bin Anas, reads it the same way: they look like one another, and the taste differs. ʿIkrimah takes the comparison to be with this world: they are similar to the fruits of this life, and the fruits of Paradise taste better. Maʿārif records both readings side by side — some commentators say the fruits resemble each other in shape while the taste changes each time, others that they resemble the fruits of the earth in shape alone with a totally different taste — and draws out the reason for the scene. What the believers are given is a joy they had never known, and it renews itself at every moment: the name and the shape stay, so that they recognise what they are being offered, and the substance is always new. Al-Mukhtaṣar states the same purpose in one clause, that they may recognise the fruit and desire it.

**A name, not a copy.**

The hardest thing said about Paradise in this verse is not in the verse, and Ibn ʿAbbās' dictum is quoted by Ibn Kathīr from al-Aʿmash: *nothing in Paradise resembles anything in the life of this world except in name* — in another narration, only the names are similar. Maʿārif takes on the reading that wants to stop there, because in his time it had become fashionable. Some modern commentators, he says, are fond of asserting that when the Qurʾān speaks of the fruits of Paradise and its other joys it is using metaphor to gesture at a spiritual bliss that is by nature intangible. He does not dismiss symbolical reading; many respected scholars, particularly among the Sufis, have offered it, and it has proved illuminating. His objection is to the confusion: no genuine Sufi claimed that analogical interpretation is the same thing as exegesis, or that his is the only valid one, since its purpose is to help a person realise something spiritually, not to cancel the plain meaning. What they miss, he says, is obvious — that a thing used as a symbol does not follow that it does not exist. The fruits of Paradise have an objective existence, though not a physical one in the sense we give the word, and their nature and state can be left to Allah. That way, in his phrase, lies security.

**What the purification covers.**

*They will have pure spouses*, and the early glosses are unsentimental about what *pure* means. Ibn Kathīr collects them: Ibn ʿAbbās, purified from filth and impurity; Mujāhid, listing what is being removed — menstruation, relieving oneself, urine, spit, semen, pregnancy; Qatādah, purified from impurity and sin, and elsewhere from menstruation and pregnancy; and ʿAṭāʾ, al-Ḥasan, al-Daḥḥāk, Abū Ṣāliḥ, ʿAtiyyah and as-Suddī reported to similar effect. Al-Jalālayn has it as houris and others, purified from menstruation and impurity; Tanwīr al-Miqbās, free of menstruation and every kind of filth. Maʿārif extends the word in a direction the others only imply, and it is the most useful thing said here: clean externally and pure internally — free from whatever is physically disgusting, and from whatever is morally disgusting, which he names as bad temper and unfaithfulness.

**Forever, and the price of it.**

The verse ends on permanence, and the sources make it the actual gift. Al-Jalālayn: they abide there forever, neither perishing nor departing from it. Ibn Kathīr: this is ultimate happiness, because the bliss is safe from death and from disruption, and it never ends or ceases. Al-Mukhtaṣar supplies the contrast the word is doing without — the joys of Paradise are unlike the joys of the earth, which are only temporary; the believer will not spend them trembling at the thought of losing them. Maʿārif draws the one hard lesson from the verse's opening words, *those who believe and do good*: the tidings come with a second condition attached, because faith alone does not earn them. Faith is enough to save a person from remaining in the Fire forever — every Muslim, however great a sinner, will be taken out once he has undergone his period of punishment — but, citing Qurṭubī's *Rūḥ al-Bayān*, that no one escapes the Fire altogether without the good deeds the law defines. Tazkīr al-Qurʾān adds the part of the reward that arrives early: those who find God in the word of God are already given a glimpse of the next world. The next verse answers a complaint about the size of the creature God chose to make an example.

26.text:
A reader objects to the Qurʾān's taste, and the Book answers by talking about gnats. *Surely Allah does not shy away from using the parable of a mosquito or what is even smaller.* Then it divides its audience in the middle of the sentence: *as for the believers, they know that it is the truth from their Lord*, and as for the others, they ask *what does Allah mean by such a parable?* The verse ends by taking the objection seriously enough to make it a test: *through this*, He says, *He leaves many to stray, and guides many.* A small creature, it turns out, is a reliable detector of what a person has already decided.

**Why the verse came down.**

Three reports in the sources agree on the occasion with slight variations. As-Suddī relays from Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd and some of the Companions that when Allah gave the two examples of the hypocrites — *their likeness is as the likeness of one who kindled a fire*, and *or like a rainstorm from the sky* (2:17, 2:19) — the hypocrites said that Allah is far more exalted than to make such examples, and these āyāt were revealed in reply. Qatādah's version, preserved by Ibn Kathīr, is more general: when Allah mentioned the fly and the spider in His Book, the people of misguidance asked why Allah had mentioned such things. Al-Jalālayn records the same cause from the other direction, at the end of the previous verse: the Jews asked what God wants with these vile creatures, and God then revealed this. Tanwīr al-Miqbās opens accordingly — Allah here mentions the objection of the Jews to the Qurʾān's similes.

**The objection, put fairly.**

Maʿārif states it as a serious aesthetic claim rather than as mockery. Had the Qurʾān been the Word of Allah, the objection runs, it would not have used contemptible creatures like an ant or a gnat in its parables, because that goes against sublimity and majesty — and it would embarrass even a man with some sense of dignity. That is the argument, and the verse takes it head-on by denying the premise it depends on: shame is a defect in the speaker, an admission that he is trying to appear better than his material. Maʿārif draws the conclusion, that doubts of this kind arise only in minds whose disbelief has drained them of the power to see things in their proper perspective, and that such misgivings never touch the hearts of believers at all. Ibn Kathīr records the same division in Mujāhid's words: the believers accept these parables whether they concern large matters or small, because they know they are the truth from their Lord, and by them Allah guides them.

**What an example is for.**

Once the purpose is a comparison, the size of the thing compared stops mattering — and the sources say so in different registers. Maʿārif: where a person intends to speak of something detestable, in a parable, the use of a gnat, or of something even more contemptible, neither transgresses the rules of eloquence and logic nor offends dignity and modesty; therefore Allah is not shy about the imagery. Tanwīr al-Miqbās brings the theological version of the same point, and it is the strongest sentence on the verse: how could He disdain mentioning a thing which, if all created beings joined forces to produce it, they would not manage? Maʿārif then generalises the ruling beyond this verse, in the section where he draws the lessons of it: if explaining something useful for people's guidance requires referring to what is thought contemptible or dirty, that is neither sinful nor blameworthy, and it does not lower the writer's dignity — and examples of exactly this disregard for ordinary modesty run through the Qurʾān, the ḥadīth, and the writings of the Sufis and other great scholars, all of them sacrificing the appearance of gravity to the object actually being pursued.

**The gnat, the thorn, and the size of a thing.**

The Arabic word is *baʿūḍah*, explained by Al-Jalālayn as the singular of *baʿūḍ*, small flies. The same source then notices that the comparative phrase in the verse is there to make size irrelevant to the judgement being made, so that the ruling is unaffected whether the creature is larger or smaller. This is worth pausing on, because the app's translation and the classical commentators run in opposite directions at this point: the commentators read the phrase as *or what is above it*, something larger than the gnat, and Tanwīr al-Miqbās supplies the expected candidates, the fly and the spider — the very two that provoked the objection — while the English here takes it as *or what is even smaller*. Either way the point stands, and Ibn Kathīr gives it a witness from the Prophet's ﷺ speech in a ḥadīth Muslim records from ʿĀʾishah: no Muslim is harmed by a thorn *or something larger*, but a good deed is written for him and an evil one erased. A word which shows that nothing is too small to carry a ruling also shows that nothing is too small to be an example. Ibn Kathīr preserves a further and stranger reading of the creature itself, from Ar-Rabīʿ bin Anas: this is an example of the life of this world, because the mosquito lives only as long as it needs its food, and dies when it grows fat — which is why Allah opens the gates of every pleasant thing on a people once they forget the warning they were given (6:44).

**The question that is not a question.**

The sources pay attention to the grammar of that question, because it is not one. Al-Jalālayn calls the interrogative here a question of rejection, and glosses the sentence as: what use is there in it? Al-Mukhtaṣar puts the same into plain words — the disbelievers make fun, asking one another why Allah would use examples with lowly creatures. What follows is the hardest clause in the verse for a modern reader, and it is deliberately so: *through this He leaves many to stray, and guides many*. Maʿārif supplies the reason, calling the parables a test: for those ready to think and to understand they become a source of guidance, and for those who refuse to understand, out of indifference or stubborn hostility and denial, they are a cause of greater confusion and misguidance. Al-Mukhtaṣar gives the mechanism in a phrase apiece — many are misguided through these examples because they refuse to consider them, and many are guided because they learn from them. Ibn Kathīr reports as-Suddī's reading that the many who stray here are the hypocrites, and that the way they are misled is precisely their own: their straying increases when they reject parables which they know in themselves to be true. The believers receive the mirror image — Allah adds guidance to their guidance and faith to their faith, because they believe firmly in what they recognise as true.

**Only the rebellious.**

*He leaves none to stray except the rebellious*, and the word is *al-fāsiqīn*, which the sources insist on defining before they use it. Maʿārif takes it from the root: *fasaqa* means to go outside, to stray beyond a limit, and in the terminology of the law *fisq* is going beyond the circle of obedience to Allah. Because transgression does not stop at disobedience in action but can harden into denial, the Qurʾān also applies the word to an outright disbeliever; and the jurists use it of a Muslim who commits a major sin without repenting, or who makes a habit of minor sins — which is why the *fāsiq* stands opposite the *kāfir*. Ibn Kathīr gives the image the Arabic keeps, without editorialising: the Arabs say of a date that it *fasaqat* when it slips out of its skin, and they call the mouse *fuwaysiqah* because it leaves its hole to do damage; the two Ṣaḥīḥ record ʿĀʾishah reporting that five animals are named *fawasiq* and may be killed while in *iḥrām* and outside it — the crow, the kite, the scorpion, the mouse and the rabid dog. A *fāsiq*, then, includes both the disbeliever and the disobedient believer, and the disbelief of the former is worse, so the verse is describing that kind of *fisq*; the proof, in Ibn Kathīr's reading, is the three marks that follow immediately — breaking Allah's covenant after it has been ratified, severing what Allah ordered to be joined, and making mischief on earth. Maʿārif adds what covenant is meant: the one made by every human being before any of them came to earth, when Allah gathered their spirits and asked, *am I not your Lord?*, and they answered, yes (7:172) — a covenant which God's books and prophets exist to renew. Which is the question the next verse takes up.

27.text:
The verse that says who the rebellious are does not open with a verb of its own. It hangs off the last words of the verse before it and lists three acts instead: *those who violate Allah's covenant after it has been affirmed, break whatever ties Allah has ordered to be maintained, and spread corruption in the land*. The three are not a random sample of bad behaviour. One is a promise broken, one is a family cut off, one is damage done to the world around them. Then comes a verdict in a single word: *it is they who are the losers*.

**Which covenant, and what "after it has been affirmed" is doing.**

Al-Jalālayn reads the covenant as a specific contract: the one God made with them in the revealed Books, to believe in Muhammad ﷺ — and he glosses *after it has been affirmed* as: after it has been confirmed with them. Tanwīr al-Miqbās piles up the synonyms of that same phrase, after sanctioning, confirming and vouchsafing it, and takes the covenant to be the one taken regarding this Prophet. Al-Mukhtaṣar goes behind that to the older pledge: the promise made with God to serve Him alone and follow His way, and he cites the verse in which the human race was made to testify — *Am I not your Lord? They said, yes, we bear witness* (7:172) — adding that God confirmed it again by sending the prophets and the scriptures. Ibn Kathīr sets the options out in order and does not force a choice. It may be Allah's covenant with his creation in general, to obey him and avoid what he prohibited, reiterated in his books and by the words of his messengers, so that ignoring it is itself the breaking of it. It was said to be about the disbelievers and hypocrites among the People of the Book, whose covenant is the pledge taken from them in the Torah to follow and believe in this Prophet when he is sent — broken when they rejected him after they knew the truth about him and hid it from people, having sworn to Allah that they would do otherwise. And it was also reported that the verse is about all disbelievers, idol-worshippers and hypocrites: Allah took their pledge to believe in his oneness by showing them the signs that testify to his lordship, and their covenant was broken when they denied what had been proven to them. Ibn Kathīr names this last interpretation, reports it from Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān, and says of it simply: it is very good — and it is also the view held by az-Zamakhsharī. Notice what all three readings have in common, and what makes this verse an indictment rather than a complaint: nobody here is accused of failing to find God. They are accused of having been told, having agreed, and then withdrawing.

**The ties in the middle.**

The second charge looks like the mildest of the three, and the sources make it the hinge. Qatādah asserted that *sever what Allah has ordered to be joined* refers to keeping relations with one's relatives, and Ibn Kathīr cites the verse where the same pairing appears — *Would you then, if you were given authority, do mischief in the land and sever your ties of kinship?* (47:22) — while Ibn Jarīr aṭ-Ṭabarī preferred that opinion. Others, he records, took the wording as more general: everything Allah commanded people to nurture, and they cut off, falls inside it. Al-Jalālayn keeps both senses at once, belief in the Prophet, kinship, and other matters. Tanwīr al-Miqbās adds oaths to the list of what is joined. Maʿārif draws the widest lesson, and it is worth reading as the summary of the verse: cutting asunder what Allah has commanded to be joined includes every kind of relationship — between Allah and his servant, between a person and his parents and relatives, between him and his neighbours and friends, between one Muslim and another, between one human being and the next. Islam, he says, means fulfilling what is owed in all of them, and that is what following the law amounts to; deficiency in those obligations produces every kind of disorder among people, which is why the transgressors end up destroying others and themselves.

**What the corruption consists of.**

*Spread corruption in the land* is left abstract in Arabic, and the sources fill it with the act of turning other people away. Tanwīr al-Miqbās: by preventing people from the religion of Muhammad ﷺ and from the Qurʾān. Al-Jalālayn: by their transgressing and by impeding faith. Tazkīr al-Qurʾān makes this the third of the duties the passage is teaching, and states it as a prohibition on argument made in bad faith — a person must not turn people away from a divine call raised by one of God's servants by inventing groundless objections to it; the message of truth is trying to harmonise a person with his own nature, and whoever prevents others from receiving it is guilty of spreading corruption in the land. That last clause explains why this verse sits exactly where it does. The chapter has just heard a man sneer at the size of a gnat, and the previous verse said that such a question is not curiosity but rejection. Now the Qurʾān tells him what his question is doing: it is the corruption. It also completes the portrait begun in verse 11, where these same people promised to be making peace and were told that they were the ones making disorder — the first accusation in the chapter, now answered with its full anatomy.

**The losers.**

Al-Jalālayn gives the outcome: they shall be the losers, since they end up in the Fire made everlasting for them. Tanwīr al-Miqbās reads the word as *the duped*, who lose this world and the Hereafter together, and Al-Mukhtaṣar says the same. Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān glosses it as meaning lost in the Hereafter. Ibn Kathīr preserves a distinction from ad-Daḥḥāk, reporting Ibn ʿAbbās: every quality that Allah says of those outside the community of Islam — being losers, for instance — refers to disbelief, but when the same words are said of Muslims they refer to sin. Which is how the chapter keeps describing the same three groups in the same three words. Ibn Jarīr aṭ-Ṭabarī explains the vocabulary itself: a loser is whoever decreases his own share of Allah's mercy by disobeying him, the way a merchant loses by taking a loss in his trade — and the disbeliever and the hypocrite lose the share of mercy stored up for Allah's servants on the Day of Resurrection. Maʿārif adds the proportion, which is the sentence to remember: real loss belongs to the other world, because the loss of this one is too small a thing to deserve serious consideration. The next verse turns from the three marks of the rebellious to the one fact that makes them indefensible — that they were not, and then they were.

28.text:
The chapter now stops arguing from the sky and starts arguing from the reader. *How can you deny Allah? You were lifeless and He gave you life.* The question is asked in a tone the sources insist on naming: it is not a request for information. Then the verse lays out a sequence — life, death, life again, and a return — and puts every stage of it outside the audience's control. Nobody in the sentence chose to be born, and nobody in it will choose the second half.

**A question with two possible tones.**

Al-Jalālayn notes that the interrogative here is either meant to provoke amazement at a persistence that the evidence has already refuted, or meant as a rebuke — and he identifies who is being addressed by naming the people of Makkah, with the same specificity he had brought to verse 21. Ibn Kathīr reads the verse as a testimony rather than a question: Allah establishes that He exists and that He is the Creator and Sustainer with full authority over his servants. The strangest part of the sentence, however, is its opening verb, and Maʿārif does not let it pass: on the face of it these people had never denied Allah at all — they had denied the Prophet ﷺ. The Qurʾān equates the two. Rejection of the messenger is not a smaller offence which happens to be related to God; it is the rejection of God, performed by the only means available to them, since this is how he has chosen to be known. Al-Mukhtaṣar puts the whole verse's mood in its first line: strange is the situation of the disbelievers — how can you deny the oneness of Allah when the signs of his power are visible in your own existence?

**What "lifeless" means.**

The Arabic word for the state they were in is *amwāt*, dead, and the sources take it with maximum literalness. Al-Jalālayn: you were dead — semen in the loins — and He gave you life in the womb and in this world by breathing the spirit into you. Tanwīr al-Miqbās completes the picture: dead sperm drops in the loins of your fathers, given life in the wombs of your mothers. Maʿārif generalises it into something harder to dismiss, glossing the state as one in which a person had no life at all: he existed, if he existed at all, as billions of lifeless particles drifting without direction, and Allah gathered them, made them into a human being, and gave them life. Ibn Kathīr reads the phrase as a move from non-existence to existence, and cites the two places where the Qurʾān presses that argument hardest: *were they created by nothing, or were they themselves the creators?* (52:35), and *has there not been over man a period of time when he was not a thing worth mentioning?* (76:1).

**Two deaths and two lives.**

The verse's four stages are not symmetrical, and one early reading makes the pattern explicit. Ibn Jarīr reported from ʿAtāʾ that Ibn ʿAbbās said of *you were dead and He gave you life*: you did not exist beforehand, you were nothing until Allah created you; then He will bring death upon you and then bring you back to life at the Resurrection — and Ibn ʿAbbās added that this is the same as the verse in which they will say, *our Lord, You have made us die twice and You have given us life twice* (40:11). Maʿārif counts the stages with the same care: the first "death" is the state before life was given, the second death comes when the allotted lifespan ends, and the second life is the Day of Judgment, when Allah will collect the scattered particles of every single person again and give him a new life. Al-Jalālayn and Tanwīr al-Miqbās both date the third term precisely — death after your term of life is completed, life again at the Resurrection.

**Death counted among the blessings.**

That is an odd thing to say, and the verse says it by putting death in a list of favours. Maʿārif states the obvious half first: according to this verse the chief blessing Allah gives a person is life, because without it no other blessing can be enjoyed at all. Then the difficult half: the verse counts death as a blessing too, because physical death is the door to the perpetual life of the world to come, after which there is no more death. He also notices where this verse stands in the chapter's design, and it repeats a pattern from earlier. Verses 21 and 22 argued from the blessings that belong to a person's own being and then from those in his environment; here again verse 28 takes up the blessing of a person's own life, and verse 29 turns to the general blessings shared with every creature — the earth and everything in it, on which life immediately depends, and the skies to which life on earth is tied. The chapter is not repeating itself for emphasis; it is offering the same proof twice, from the two places a person can actually check it.

**And then to Him you will be returned.**

The final clause is the one the audience objected to most, and Al-Jalālayn says so flatly: Allah states this as a proof of the Resurrection, at a time when they denied it. The evidence for something they thought absurd is that the first half of it happened without their help. Maʿārif spells the return out: all people will rise from their graves, be assembled to give an account of their deeds, and be rewarded or punished for what they were doing. Al-Mukhtaṣar adds the word the others assume, that they will then be held accountable, and Tanwīr al-Miqbās that He will requite them for their works. But the verse has been careful about what it is asking for, and Maʿārif closes on that. If these people will not take the trouble to consider the arguments the chapter has already advanced, then there is a shorter road open to anyone whose nature has not been ruined: be grateful to the one who benefited you. Gratitude, on his reading, is not a devotional decoration here. It is a way of arriving, by the simplest possible route, at why you should obey. The next verse begins that route — *He it is Who created for you everything on the earth*.
